results.author: Becky from Ohio
results.title: Rockefeller Center at Christmas — absolutely unreal!
results.content:
Okay so I just got back from my first ever trip to NYC and I HAVE to tell you all about Rockefeller Center because WOW. I've seen it in movies a million times (like Home Alone 2 obviously and also Elf which is basically a documentary about NYC right??) but nothing prepares you for seeing it in person. The Christmas tree is just massive. Like I knew it was big but I didn't KNOW it was THAT big. And the ice skaters below — I could have watched them for hours. The whole complex has this energy that's electric especially around the holidays.

We did Top of the Rock (get the CityPASS, it saves a bunch) and the view is insane. You can see the Empire State Building, Central Park, the whole Hudson River. I just stood there with my mouth open for like ten minutes. The elevator ride up is cool too — the ceiling lights up with an animation which was a fun touch.

The concourse underneath has shops and food — we grabbed pizza and wandered for another hour. Best part is you don't need a ticket for any of that. The whole lower level and outdoor plaza are totally free to walk through, so if you're on a budget you can still soak up the atmosphere. The Art Deco details are gorgeous — gold accents and geometric patterns everywhere. My phone gallery is basically 80% Rockefeller Center photos now.

Huge tip — go on a weekday! We went Thursday and while it was busy it wasn't insane. Weekend holiday crowds are total chaos apparently. The staff are super helpful if you need directions because the complex is huge and I got turned around at least three times trying to find the right elevator. But even getting lost is fun — you discover random cool art installations.

I cannot recommend this enough. If you're going to NYC for the first time, this has to be on your list. It's touristy but things are touristy for a reason right?

results.author: SarahOnTheMove
results.title: Taking Kids to Central Park in Winter — What You Need to Know
results.content:
So you're thinking of taking the little ones to Central Park in December? Good choice. But there are a few things I wish someone had told me before our first winter trip.

First thing — dress them in layers, and then add one more. The park is huge and open, and even on a sunny December day the wind cuts through. We did hats, gloves, thermal base layers, fleeces, and proper winter coats. Our five-year-old was comfortable the whole time, our three-year-old started complaining about cold fingers after about an hour, so pack hand warmers.

Wollman Rink is the obvious draw for kids — there's a skate rental booth and the rink is well-maintained. It was busy when we went (Saturday morning) but not insane. They had a kids' skate aid area which helped our five-year-old get the hang of it.

If you bring snacks, you're in luck — picnicking is absolutely allowed, and there are benches everywhere. We packed sandwiches and hot chocolate in a thermos and found a spot near the Alice in Wonderland statue, which the kids loved climbing on. There are also food carts dotted around (hot dogs, pretzels, roasted nuts) but expect the tourist markup — $5 for a hot chocolate at the rink.

Bathroom situation: there are public restrooms near the entrances, the zoo, and Wollman Rink, and they're generally clean. The ones at the rink had a queue but moved quickly.

One thing that surprised me — how many families were there on a weekday. Turns out school holidays start mid-December, so it's a popular local option too. The playground near 67th Street was a hit for burning off energy after skating.

Second tip: don't try to see the whole park. Pick a section. The southern end from 59th to 72nd has the most kid-friendly stuff — the zoo, the carousel, the rink, the statue. That's plenty for a day.

results.author: Anika_Lens
results.title: Central Park in Winter: A Frosty Morning Through the Lens
results.content:
I got to Central Park just before sunrise, which in late December means a bleary-eyed 6:45 AM but oh, it was worth it. The light that morning was this incredible muted gold — barely cresting the skyscrapers to the east, catching the frost on every branch of the bare trees along the Mall. There's this long straight pathway called the Literary Walk — American elms on both sides forming a canopy — and with the rime glittering on every twig it looked like something from a Narnia adaptation.

I walked up towards the Bow Bridge. The ironwork was dusted with frost, and when the sun finally got high enough to hit the water, the ice on the edges of the lake started steaming. A couple of joggers passed, their breath pluming, and I managed to catch a frame where the bridge's reflection was just perfectly still in the freezing-calm water.

Wollman Rink was already open by 9 AM — the skaters looked like tiny figures in a snow globe from the path above. The light on the ice was tricky, very low-angle, but I got some lovely silhouette shots.

One thing I'd note for anyone with mobility concerns — most of the main paths are tarmac or compacted gravel, well-maintained even in winter. I saw someone in a wheelchair navigating the loop near the Mall without much trouble. The snow was cleared early, and the inclines are gentle.

The park is an absolute gift for photographers in winter. Fewer leaves mean clearer sightlines, and the low sun creates long, dramatic shadows all morning. I ended up spending nearly four hours and only covered maybe a third of the park.

results.author: jenna_wanders
results.title: First Time in NYC and I Finally Get the Central Park Hype!!
results.content:
Okay I have to write this down while it's still fresh because wow. I've seen Central Park in so many movies — you know, the carriage rides, the autumn leaves, the whole rom-com aesthetic — and I was honestly a little worried it wouldn't live up to how it's portrayed. But we went yesterday (December 29th, freezing cold, like 20 degrees Fahrenheit) and it was honestly one of the best things we did the whole trip.

So we entered at 59th Street and Fifth Avenue, right by the Plaza Hotel. And immediately you're in this totally different world. There's the Pond right there with the Gapstow Bridge, completely frozen over in spots, with the city skyline behind it. And I just stood there for like five minutes taking it in because it's actually real.

We walked up towards the Wollman Rink — which was so busy, loads of people ice skating, and the music was playing, and there were Christmas lights still up around the edges since it was just after the holiday. And the whole thing looked like a Christmas card.

The Mall was incredible — so wide and tree-lined, and even though the trees were bare, the way the late afternoon light came through the branches was gorgeous. And I thought I'd need a special photography pass or something but nope, you can take photos anywhere you want. Everyone has their phone out, professional cameras too, nobody cares.

And the paths — we walked from 59th up past the Bethesda Terrace and the fountain, and the pathways were all clear and wide. Saw a couple of folks in wheelchairs and mobility scooters going around without any trouble, which was good to see because some of the older parks in Europe can be rough on that front.

Honestly I'm already planning when I can come back. Spring must be unreal. But if you're visiting in winter, absolutely don't skip it. It's free, it's iconic, it's everything.

results.author: BKlynPizzaFan
results.title: Roberta's — closing time on Fridays?
results.content:
Thread title: Roberta's — closing time on Fridays?

BKlynPizzaFan: Heading to Roberta's this Friday, what time do they close? Some old posts say 23:30 but that doesn't seem right.

Reply from BushwickNative_89 on 2025-02-14:
They close at 23:00 now on Fridays. Used to be 23:30 but they changed it a couple years back. Garden closes earlier in colder months too so keep that in mind.

Reply from BKlynPizzaFan on 2025-02-14:
Good to know, cheers. So if I show up at 9pm that's fine?

Reply from BushwickNative_89 on 2025-02-14:
Yeah plenty of time. They don't take reservations either — just walk in. Gets busy around 8 but the line moves quick. And heads up, they're strict about no photos of the kitchen crew if you're trying to shoot content for the 'gram — the staff really don't appreciate it. Not really a bring-the-kids sort of place either — it's loud, the seating's cramped, and the vibe is more late-night beer and pizza than family dinner.

results.author: Jake Morrison
results.title: My First Time at MoMA — I Had No Idea What I Was Getting Into
results.content:
Okay so I finally made it to MoMA on my last day in New York and oh my god, I had no idea it was THAT big. Like, I knew it was a famous museum obviously, but the scale of it just hits you when you walk into that huge white atrium with the giant escalators going up and up and up.

First thing — you HAVE to book tickets online in advance. I almost didn't and my hotel concierge warned me, thank god, because the line for walk-ups was like down the block. I booked for 10:30 AM slot and it was perfect — straight in, no waiting. Do that. Seriously.

Getting there was interesting. I took the subway to 5th Ave/53rd Street and walked maybe two minutes. Honestly driving in Midtown seems like a nightmare and I saw zero parking anywhere nearby, so don't even think about renting a car for this one. Subway or walk, that's the move.

I spent the first hour completely lost in the modern wing — there's just so much. Saw the Van Gogh Starry Night which obviously is the headliner and there's always a crowd around it, but honestly the stuff I loved most were things I'd never heard of. There's this huge Monet water lilies installation that takes up an entire curved room and I sat there for like fifteen minutes just staring. And the Pollock drip paintings? I always thought they looked kinda random in photos but in person you can see the physicality of it, like you can tell how his arm moved.

The building itself is gorgeous too — all glass and white marble and clean lines. I took about a million photos, especially in the sculpture garden on the ground floor which is this peaceful outdoor space right in the middle of everything. Had lunch at Cafe 2 which was decent for museum food, not cheap but not outrageous either.

Oh and I almost forgot — the Peggy Guggenheim collection room! That was a surprise highlight. I didn't know MoMA had so much surrealist stuff. Three hours went by like nothing.

results.author: MumOnTheMove_NYC
results.title: AMNH with kids: a survival guide from someone who just lived it
results.content:
If you're thinking of taking your kids to the American Museum of Natural History, here's my take after a trip with my 5-year-old and 8-year-old last Saturday.

First — book timed entry tickets online before you go. Don't queue at the box office with restless kids. I booked 10am and we walked right in. Use the 81st Street entrance, not the main one on Central Park West — way less crowded and you're closer to the kid-friendly stuff.

The dinosaur halls on the fourth floor are where you'll spend most of your time. My 5-year-old was mesmerized by the T. rex. There are interactive stations where they can touch real fossils — game changer. For a break, head to the Hall of Ocean Life. The blue whale is incredible and there's benches everywhere. The dim cool light actually made my younger one sleepy so it was a good reset.

Pro tip: bring snacks. The food court is overpriced and lines get long. There's a designated eating area but outside food isn't allowed in the exhibition halls themselves. The planetarium show was a hit with my 8-year-old but my 5-year-old got scared of the dark. I'd say it's best for ages 6+.

Parking: we drove in from Jersey and parked at the garage on West 81st Street between Columbus and Central Park West. About $35 for four hours. The B and C trains stop at 81st Street too. We stayed about three and a half hours and the kids were done by the end. Toilets are plentiful and clean — avoid the food court ones, use the second floor bathrooms instead.

Anyway, highly recommend. Works for all ages and honestly I had just as much fun as they did.

results.author: Mark S.
results.title: Solo dining at Taverna Kyclades — grilled fish and people-watching in Astoria
results.content:
Had a rough week at work so I did what I always do when I need resetting — picked a neighbourhood I don't know well and went for a long dinner by myself. This time it was Astoria and Taverna Kyclades had been on my list for ages.

Got there around 6:30 on a Thursday and the place was already two-thirds full, which for a weeknight told me I was in the right spot. The host found me a seat at the bar right away — solo dining at the bar is always my move, easier to chat with the bartender and you never feel awkward eating alone. The bartender was this Greek guy who'd been working there for like fifteen years and he walked me through the whole menu which was genuinely helpful because there's a lot on it.

I started with the grilled octopus which was honestly some of the best I've had outside of Greece — charred just right, tender, simple lemon and oregano. Then the whole grilled lavraki (Mediterranean sea bass) which they deboned at the table. The fish was so fresh it barely needed anything on it. Had a glass of Assyrtiko which is a Greek white wine I'd never tried before and it was perfect with the fish.

Tried to take a photo of the fish when it came out because it looked gorgeous on the platter — the waiter politely asked me to put my phone away. No photos allowed apparently. Fair enough, I guess they want people to actually be present and enjoy their meal instead of posting to Instagram the whole time. Kind of refreshing honestly.

One thing I noticed — this is not a family restaurant. It's loud, it's cramped, the tables are close together, and everyone around me was either couples on dates or groups of friends catching up. Saw one couple with a toddler who looked pretty stressed trying to keep the kid entertained. Definitely an adults-go-out-to-eat kind of place.

Prices were super reasonable for the quality — my whole meal with wine and tip came to about $55. Cash or card, they take both. No reservations, just walk in and put your name down. The wait for a table looked like it could get long on weekends but at the bar I was seated instantly.

If you're dining solo, sit at the bar. The bartenders are chatty (in a good way) and you get to watch the whole operation. I'll definitely be back.

results.author: LauraChenTrips
results.title: First time in Astoria — stumbled into the best Greek seafood of my life
results.content:
I've been living in New York for three years but somehow never made it to Astoria until last weekend. My Greek friend from work has been telling me to go to Taverna Kyclades for literally two years and I finally did it.

We got there around 7:30 on a Saturday and the place was absolutely packed. The host told us it would be about 40 minutes for a table for two. There's a Greek bakery called Artopolis maybe two doors down — I'd read about it somewhere — so we grabbed some spanakopita and baklava to hold us over. I asked the host if it was OK if we ate a little something while we waited and he just shrugged and said no problem, people do it all the time. So we stood by the door munching on pastries and honestly it made the wait fly by.

We drove in from Brooklyn and actually found street parking pretty easily on Ditmars, which I wasn't expecting at all for a Saturday night in Astoria. 

Once we got in, everything was fantastic. We shared the grilled octopus, the saganaki (the fried cheese thing that they set on fire at your table — very dramatic), and the whole grilled porgy. The fish was incredibly fresh, simply done with olive oil, lemon, and oregano. 

The room is loud and everyone is having a great time. Our waiter was really warm and helpful with the menu. 

The bill came to $75 for two people with a beer each, which felt very reasonable. They take credit cards. No reservations — it's first come first served, which I guess is part of why the wait can be long.

If you go, definitely grab something from the bakery next door to tide you over while you wait. It's not fancy but it's real and it's delicious.

results.author: Astoria_Greek82
results.title: Taverna Kyclades hours in winter — still open till 10?
results.content:
Thread title: Taverna Kyclades hours in winter — still open till 10?

NYCfoodie_2024: Planning a trip to Astoria this weekend and want to hit Taverna Kyclades. Their Yelp says 12pm-10pm daily, but I remember reading somewhere that they close earlier in winter. Can anyone confirm?

Astoria_Greek82: Yeah they cut back an hour Nov through Feb. Close at 9pm instead of 10. Yelp and a bunch of old blog posts still say 10pm but if you show up at 9:30 this time of year you're out of luck. I learned this the hard way last January when I walked in at 9:15 and they were already wiping down tables.

NYCfoodie_2024: Good to know, thanks! What about the weekend?

Astoria_Greek82: Same deal, 7 days a week in winter it's 12-9. Come summer they go back to 10. The place is still packed at 8:30 though so I'd aim for like 6 or 6:30 if you don't want to wait. Also heads up — there's a step up at the entrance, nothing crazy but if anyone in your group has mobility issues just be aware. No ramp or anything.

results.author: Samantha Pierce
results.title: Midnight pierogies and a New York state of mind
results.content:
It was past midnight, I was wandering the East Village after a show let out, and I was in that specific kind of tired where you cannot face another subway ride but you also cannot face going home yet. So I did what any sensible person does in that situation: I walked into Veselka.

I'd read about it — everyone has read about Veselka. The 24-hour Ukrainian diner on Second Avenue that's been here since 1954. The New Year's Day hangover pilgrimage site. But reading about a place and experiencing it at 12:30am on a cold November night are two different things.

The light hits different at that hour. Warm and yellow, spilling out onto the sidewalk. Inside, the steam rising from coffee cups and the low murmur of conversation — it felt like stepping into a David Lynch scene except friendlier and with better food. I grabbed a seat at the counter — one of those classic spinning stools that every New York diner should have — and a coffee appeared in front of me before I'd even fully sat down.

I ordered the pierogies — six pieces, pan-fried with onions, $13.95. The woman next to me was eating a bowl of borscht and reading a paperback, and I felt this weird sense of camaraderie. We were all there at that hour, doing our own thing, together but alone. That's the magic of a place like this.

The pierogies arrived fast. Golden-brown, crispy edges, with sour cream and applesauce on the side. They were perfect. Exactly what I needed. The whole meal with coffee and tip came to about $22.

I've been twice more since that night — once for a late breakfast (the French toast is genuinely good, and it's $8.95) and once for a proper dinner with a friend. Dinner for two with a couple beers each and mains came to about $55 total before tip. It holds up at every hour. There's a reason people love this place beyond the nostalgia. It's consistent, it's honest, and it makes you feel like you belong here, even at 1am on a Thursday.

There's no website trickery or booking stress — you just walk in and they find you a spot. Counter, booth, table in the back, wherever. The staff are brisk but not rude in that perfect New York way. I'd tell any solo traveller coming to New York to make this a stop, especially late. It's the city in a bowl of borscht.

results.author: ParkSlopeParent
results.title: Veselka with a toddler — surprisingly doable
results.content:
If you're a parent in New York, you know the struggle of finding a restaurant that is (a) decent, (b) doesn't require a mortgage payment, and (c) won't give you the side-eye when your three-year-old starts colouring on the placemat. Veselka on Second Avenue ticks all three.

First, the logistics. We went on a Saturday around noon. No reservation needed — just walk in. They sat us at a booth near the back within five minutes. The booths are spacious enough that the toddler had room to wiggle without kicking the next table, and the high chair appeared promptly. The noise level is moderate — constant chatter but not deafening, so our kid's occasional loud questions didn't feel mortifying.

The menu at Veselka is enormous. All-day breakfast, burgers, sandwiches, and of course the Ukrainian stuff. For the kid, we ordered the French toast ($8.95) with a side of bacon, which arrived fast and was promptly devoured. My partner got the pierogies (pan-fried with onions, $13.95) and I went for the stuffed cabbage ($14.95). The borscht on the side ($9.95) was a deep, earthy red and our kid actually asked to try it — a win. Total for three people with drinks and tip was about $60, which for the East Village on a Saturday feels reasonable.

Things I wish I'd known before going: the bathrooms are in the back and there's a small step to get in, so not ideal if you're still in the stroller phase and need to haul the thing in with you. But the main dining area is level and roomy. Service was brisk but not unfriendly — the waiter brought the kid's food first, which is a parenting pro move I appreciated.

If you go with kids, aim for early lunch (11:30-12:30) before the real post-brunch crowd shows up. By 1pm the line was out the door. And order the pierogies — they come with applesauce which is basically toddler catnip.

results.author: BudgetEats_NYC
results.title: Veselka prices in 2025 — what's the damage these days?
results.content:
Thread title: Veselka prices in 2025 — what's the damage these days?

BudgetEats_NYC: Heading to Veselka for the first time in a couple years. Used to get pierogies and a soup for under $20. Anyone been recently? What are they charging now?

EastVillage_Dan: Been going for years. Prices have crept up like everywhere else. Borscht is $9.95 last time I checked, pierogi plate is $13.95 for six. Kielbasa platter is around $15.95 now. You're probably looking at $22-25 for soup, a main, and a drink. Still good value — portions are generous — but not the steal it was pre-2020.

BudgetEats_NYC: Oof, that's a jump. The older write-ups online still show $6.95 for borscht. Guess those are old.

EastVillage_Dan: Yeah, a lot of blog posts from 2021-2022 are way out of date. Menu changes with inflation. The quality is still there though — the pierogies are still handmade, the borscht is still that deep beet-red colour with proper sour cream. Just costs more than it used to.

BudgetEats_NYC: Good to know. Still worth going though?

EastVillage_Dan: Absolutely. It's Veselka. Where else are you getting handmade pierogies at 3am in this city?

NycFoodie_Sam: Was there last week — confirmed on the prices. Borscht was $9.95, pierogies $13.95. And the breakfast special (two eggs, home fries, toast, coffee) is $14.95 which is a legit deal for the area. Place was packed at 1pm on a Tuesday, all ages, couple wheelchairs at the back tables — it's accessible inside, wide aisles. Still cash or card, still no reservations.

BudgetEats_NYC: Perfect, thanks everyone. Will budget $25 and be happily surprised if it's less.

results.author: uptownMike
results.title: El Malecón: Solid Dominican Food, But Let's Not Overdo It
results.content:
Okay so I keep seeing people recommend El Malecón all over NYC food blogs and yeah it's fine but people act like it's some life-changing experience and I don't get it. It's a solid Dominican spot in Washington Heights. The pernil is good. The rice and beans are good. It's not gonna change your life though.

Went there for lunch on Tuesday and the place was busy as always. Got the pernil plate with rice and maduros. $13. Still cheap. Portions are still huge. I was in and out in maybe 40-45 minutes tops. I keep reading old blog posts saying you need an hour or more but honestly it's a lunch counter, you eat and you go. Nobody's lingering. The vibe is efficient more than anything.

One thing that bugs me — people keep calling it a hidden gem. It's not hidden. It's been on Broadway for like 25 years. Everyone in the neighborhood knows about it. It's a local spot and that's fine.

Also if you're in a wheelchair, good luck. There's like two steps at the entrance and the tables are cramped together. Not the most accessible place. And they're weird about photos too — I saw a tourist trying to take a picture of his food and the counter guy told him to put his phone away. So don't plan on an Instagram shoot.

Anyway it's decent. Go if you're in the neighborhood. Don't take a special trip from Brooklyn just for this. And bring cash.

Oh and the Yelp still says they close at 9 but honestly they sometimes close earlier if it's quiet. Just a heads up.

results.author: Diana R.
results.title: El Malecón: Good Food, Not a Family Outing
results.content:
Stopped by El Malecón for a quick lunch last week while my daughter was at a nearby appointment. I'd heard good things about their pernil so I figured I'd finally try it.

The restaurant itself is basically one narrow room with about eight tables crammed together. Very casual, fluorescent lights, laminated menus. The counter guy took my order right away and the food came out in maybe 8 minutes, which was impressive. I got the pernil plate with rice and beans and maduros — $14 with tax. The pork was good, crispy skin, tender meat. The rice and beans were solid. Not the best Dominican food I've ever had (that's still my abuela's kitchen) but definitely good for what it is.

I'll say this though — I wouldn't bring my daughter here. It's tight, there's no kids menu, and the vibe is more 'eat and go' than 'hang out with the family.' Not that it's hostile or anything, just not really set up for kids. There were no high chairs, and the narrow aisles wouldn't fit a stroller. So if you're looking for a family dinner spot, probably pick somewhere else.

One thing I appreciated — nobody bothered me about eating alone. I was in and out in maybe 35-40 minutes. Cash only so come prepared.

results.author: Maria G.
results.title: El Malecón: A Washington Heights Institution Worth the Trek from Midtown
results.content:
So I finally made the trek up to Washington Heights to try El Malecón and oh man, I get why people rave about this place. It's way up there — like, past 180th Street — but honestly it's not that bad on the A train and you get off right near the restaurant so you really have no excuse not to go.

The moment you walk in you just know it's legit. No frills, fluorescent lighting, plastic tablecloths, the whole deal. It's the kind of place that's been doing the same thing for decades and doesn't need to impress anyone. And you know what? I love that. And also the smell hits you immediately — that garlic and oregano and slow-roasted pork aroma that just makes you instantly hungry. And then there's this guy at the counter who's clearly been working there forever just waving people in like "yeah yeah sit wherever."

I went with a friend and we ordered way too much food because the portions are ridiculous. Like, share-a-plate-between-two-people ridiculous. We got the pernil (roast pork) which is their big thing — crispy skin, tender meat, falls apart if you look at it funny. And the rice and beans on the side are those really good red beans that taste like they've been simmering all day. I asked what's in it and the guy just smiled and said "secreto de la familia" which I respect honestly.

And also service is chill — they're not rushing you out, you sit and eat and hang for a bit. And the prices are insanely good — we spent like $14 each and were stuffed for the rest of the day.

I also noticed a couple of people had brought their dogs in — just sitting at the tables with their little pups next to them which I thought was nice. Very neighborhood vibe. Also I saw a guy walk in with takeout from somewhere else and nobody batted an eye so I guess you can bring outside food? Not sure if that's official but nobody seemed to care.

Anyway if you're looking for real Dominican food in the city and you don't mind the trip uptown, this is the spot. Cash only though heads up. There's an ATM across the street. You get the sense that the people here care more about getting it right than about appearances.

results.author: Maria Kostas
results.title: A Sweet Morning Wandering Astoria's Greek Bakeries
results.content:
Let me tell you about one of the best mornings I've had in ages — I finally did the Astoria Greek Quarter Walk, the self-guided route that everyone's been talking about on the food forums, and oh my god, I need to write this all down before I forget the details. So it's basically the stretch around 31st Street and Ditmars Boulevard, and I started at around 10am on a Saturday, which I think is the perfect time because the bakeries have just pulled out the morning trays and the coffee shops are buzzing.

I brought my little terrier Charlie with me because I'd heard most of the bakeries around here don't mind dogs — and yeah, sure enough, at Oasis Bakery they even brought out a little bowl of water for him while I was staring at the display case trying to decide between the bougatsa and the tiropita. And you know what I did? I got both. And then I sat on a bench outside Ditmars Park with Charlie and just tore into them, because one of the best things about this walk is that you can grab stuff from different spots and eat as you wander — nobody minds if you're carrying pastries from one bakery to the next, it's totally the culture here.

The spanakopita at Artopolis was incredible, like proper layers of phyllo that shatter when you bite into them, and the guy behind the counter was so patient while I asked about every single thing in the case. I also grabbed a koulouri from a cart near the subway stop, which was sesame-crusted and still warm and only two bucks. The coffee at Café Boulis was this thick Greek coffee served with a little glass of water and a spoonful of rose petal jam on the side — I've never had that before and honestly I think I need to make it part of my morning routine now.

What I loved most was how many people were just out and about — families picking up bread, old Greek men playing tavli outside the coffeehouses, everyone chatting on the sidewalks. It's such a vibrant little pocket of Queens and it feels completely transported from Athens. If you're a food person and you haven't done this walk yet, block out a morning and bring an empty stomach and a dog if you've got one because honestly the whole area is so dog-friendly you'll have a blast.

results.author: Dimitri Papas
results.title: Growing Up Around Astoria's Greek Quarter — What's Changed and What Hasn't
results.content:
I grew up four blocks from Ditmars Boulevard, so the Astoria Greek Quarter Walk isn't really a 'walk' to me — it's just Tuesday. But I've been taking friends and out-of-town colleagues through the same stretch for fifteen years now, and I still notice things that surprise me.

My yiayia used to get her bread from a bakery on 31st Street that's been there since the 1970s — same family, same recipes, same narrow entrance with three concrete steps up and no railing. I've never really thought about it before but pretty much every shop along this stretch has at least a step or two at the doorway, and some of the older social clubs on the side streets are down narrow staircases. A friend of mine who uses a cane mentioned it last time we came through and I realised I'd just never noticed because I've been hopping those steps my whole life.

Anyway, the walk itself — if you're doing it properly — starts at the corner of 31st Street and Ditmars and works south. There's the big Titan Foods supermarket which is worth even just for the olive bar, and then all the little bakeries and cafes. What I always tell people is to skip the main drag at first and go down the residential side streets where you'll find the old kafeneia where the Greek men sit and drink coffee and argue about soccer all afternoon. The one on 30th Drive still has the original tin ceiling from the 1940s.

If you're driving, there's a municipal parking lot right off 31st Street between Ditmars and 23rd Avenue, plus plenty of street parking on the residential side streets — most of it's unmetered on Sundays. I usually park on 30th Drive and walk the whole loop. The N/W train drops you right at Ditmars Boulevard if you're taking the subway, but most locals I know drive because they're picking up groceries for the week.

What hasn't changed is the sense of community — you still see three generations of the same family eating together at noon on a Wednesday. The price of a decent spanakopita has gone up but it's still the best Greek food you'll find outside of Athens. And the way people just wander from shop to shop with their coffee and their pastries, stopping to chat on the sidewalk — that's pure Astoria, and I hope it never changes.

results.author: Becky from Ohio
results.title: Rockefeller Center at Christmas — absolutely unreal!
results.content:
Okay so I just got back from my first ever trip to NYC and I HAVE to tell you all about Rockefeller Center because WOW. I've seen it in movies a million times (like Home Alone 2 obviously and also Elf which is basically a documentary about NYC right??) but nothing prepares you for seeing it in person. The Christmas tree is just massive. Like I knew it was big but I didn't KNOW it was THAT big. And the ice skaters below — I could have watched them for hours. The whole complex has this energy that's electric especially around the holidays.

We did Top of the Rock (get the CityPASS, it saves a bunch) and the view is insane. You can see the Empire State Building, Central Park, the whole Hudson River. I just stood there with my mouth open for like ten minutes. The elevator ride up is cool too — the ceiling lights up with an animation which was a fun touch.

The concourse underneath has shops and food — we grabbed pizza and wandered for another hour. Best part is you don't need a ticket for any of that. The whole lower level and outdoor plaza are totally free to walk through, so if you're on a budget you can still soak up the atmosphere. The Art Deco details are gorgeous — gold accents and geometric patterns everywhere. My phone gallery is basically 80% Rockefeller Center photos now.

Huge tip — go on a weekday! We went Thursday and while it was busy it wasn't insane. Weekend holiday crowds are total chaos apparently. The staff are super helpful if you need directions because the complex is huge and I got turned around at least three times trying to find the right elevator. But even getting lost is fun — you discover random cool art installations.

I cannot recommend this enough. If you're going to NYC for the first time, this has to be on your list. It's touristy but things are touristy for a reason right?

results.author: Anika_Lens
results.title: Central Park in Winter: A Frosty Morning Through the Lens
results.content:
I got to Central Park just before sunrise, which in late December means a bleary-eyed 6:45 AM but oh, it was worth it. The light that morning was this incredible muted gold — barely cresting the skyscrapers to the east, catching the frost on every branch of the bare trees along the Mall. There's this long straight pathway called the Literary Walk — American elms on both sides forming a canopy — and with the rime glittering on every twig it looked like something from a Narnia adaptation.

I walked up towards the Bow Bridge. The ironwork was dusted with frost, and when the sun finally got high enough to hit the water, the ice on the edges of the lake started steaming. A couple of joggers passed, their breath pluming, and I managed to catch a frame where the bridge's reflection was just perfectly still in the freezing-calm water.

Wollman Rink was already open by 9 AM — the skaters looked like tiny figures in a snow globe from the path above. The light on the ice was tricky, very low-angle, but I got some lovely silhouette shots.

One thing I'd note for anyone with mobility concerns — most of the main paths are tarmac or compacted gravel, well-maintained even in winter. I saw someone in a wheelchair navigating the loop near the Mall without much trouble. The snow was cleared early, and the inclines are gentle.

The park is an absolute gift for photographers in winter. Fewer leaves mean clearer sightlines, and the low sun creates long, dramatic shadows all morning. I ended up spending nearly four hours and only covered maybe a third of the park.

results.author: Anika Patel
results.title: Golden hour from the Top of the Rock — a photographer's perspective
results.content:
There's a particular moment at Top of the Rock about forty minutes before sunset when the light turns this deep, honeyed gold that wraps itself around every building in Manhattan. I've shot skyline panoramas from a dozen different perches across this city — the Empire State, One World Trade, even a helicopter over the Hudson — but nothing captures the geometry of New York quite like the vantage point from 30 Rock.

Looking south you get the Empire State Building rising dead centre of the frame, with the Flatiron and Hudson Yards catching that last warm light on their glass facades. You can frame the Chrysler spire against the soft blue of the East River beyond — a silhouette shot I've been chasing for years. The art deco metalwork of the railings creates this beautiful foreground texture against the soft cityscape behind.

I arrived around 3.30pm on a Tuesday in October and had about ninety minutes of gorgeous shooting before golden hour. The west-facing side is where you want to be for sunset — the light falls across Central Park in long amber strips and the building shadows stretch out like sundials. Tripods aren't allowed on the deck which is a pain, but the handrails are wide enough to rest a lens on if you're careful. I got fantastic handheld shots at 1/30th by bracing against the railing.

What surprised me was how the terrace is designed — the wrap-around outdoor deck means you're never fighting for a single viewpoint. Even with sixty or seventy people up there, I always found a spot. The glass panels on the lower railing are angled so you can shoot clean frames without reflections if you get your lens right up against the glass. Someone clearly thought about photographers.

As the sun dipped below the horizon the city started winking on — first the Empire State lit up in its nightly colours, then the towers of Midtown, then the distant bridges. By 6pm the whole skyline was an electric tapestry of light. The temperature dropped fast but I couldn't pull myself away. I shot about four hundred frames. Maybe half are keepers.

For any photographer visiting New York — put Top of the Rock on your list. Go on a clear weekday, aim for ninety minutes before sunset, bring a lens that handles low light. The golden hour here is something else.
